newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - LVMH unveils merger plan, gets cool reaction.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LVMH unveils merger plan, gets cool reaction.

text.p: French drinks and luxury goods firm LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton on Wednesday unveiled a plan for a mega drinks merger with British group Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc.
The proposal is part of LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's attempt to block a separate merger plan of the two British groups alone which would have left LVMH on the sidelines.
Guinness and GrandMet said they would study the plan. In a first reaction they called the plan "complicated and costly".

Under Arnault's plan a new company, to be listed in Paris and London, would be a world leader with 19 of the 100 best known wines and spirits brands. These would include Moet & Chandon and Pommery champagnes, Hennessy cognacs, the Johnny Walker, Dewar and J&B whisky brands as well as Smirnoff vodka and Baileys cream.
The company would have had proforma sales of 7.4 billion stg ($12.4 billion) for the year 1995/1996.
LVMH shares originally jumped on the statement, which had been expected after Arnault had meetings with Guinness head Tony Greener and George Bull of Grand Metropolitan earlier this month.
But after the British brush-off, shares cut their gains. At 1445 GMT, LVMH was up 2.98 percent at 1,626 francs.
The two British companies, in which LVMH has stakes of 14.2 and 6.4 percent respectively, in May announced their own plan to merge a wider group of activities, creating a company called GMG Brands.
LVMH proposes the merger of its Moet Hennessy cognac and champagnes business with the United Distillers (UD) division of Guinness and International Distillers & Vintners (IDV) of Grand Met.
LVMH would have a stake of some 35 percent in the new grouping, in exchange for its 66 percent stake in Moet Hennessy and its holdings in Guinness and GrandMet.
London analysts called this stake too high, with Mark Puleikis of Merill Lynch saying a stake of 27 percent was the maximum. French analysts said they had expected a stake of 30 to 35 percent

Shareholders in Guinness and GrandMet would get 60 pence per share, shares in the new group as well as shares in three new listed companies that will hold respectively the food, fast food and beer activities of the two British groups.
LVMH added that if its plan was adopted, arbitrage concerning a buyout of Guinness's stakes in joint ventures of the two companies as well as the 34 percent in Moet Hennessy would be dropped.
LVMH had claimed that the May merger plan was a "control event" which allowed it to buy back the stakes from Guinness at a discount.

Arnault said in the statement that his plan offered a number of advantages for shareholders over the GMG Brands plan. He said there would be synergies between the joint-venture companies of Guinness and LVMH with IDV units.
He said there would be a redistribution of brand portfolios between companies belonging to LVMH, UD and IDV. He also said that there would be bigger cost savings.

"The product line-up (of Guinness and GrandMet) will be enlarged with the introduction of high-end products (champagne and cognac) and a wider geographical coverage, mainly in Asia, which will allow an increase in sales and margins of the products," LVMH said in the statement.

LVMH added that the creation of new companies for wines and spirits, food, fastfood and beer would create "indepedently listed companies which will not suffer from a discount applied to shares of a conglomerate uniting all these activities."
The separate food unit under LVMH's plan would include GrandMet's U.S. food arm Pillsbury which has such brands as Green Giant.
The fast food unit would mainly include the Burger King hamburger chain of GrandMet while the brewing unit would produce the epynomous Guinness dark stout.
